beats.say: In 1905, Lord Curzon unveiled a new railway line, slicing the fertile Ganges delta like a wound.
The line favored Calcutta's British merchants, starving eastern ports of trade and stirring Bengali merchants' fury.
Sensing revolt, the Viceroy redrew provincial borders, pairing Muslim East Bengal with Hindu West in a single stroke.
But the railway's true purpose was to move troops quickly, anticipating a nationalist uprising in Dhaka.
Local newspapers whispered that the line's steel rails were forged from confiscated Indian gold, a myth that fanned anger.
When the partition took effect on October 16, villages found themselves split, families forced to cross the new border daily.
The British police erected checkpoints on the railway, turning trains into moving prisons for dissenting scholars.
Meanwhile, secret societies used the same tracks to smuggle revolutionary pamphlets from Dhaka to Calcutta.
By 1906, the railway became the battlefield of ideas, where loyalty and rebellion clanged like steel.
The line's ghost still haunts modern Bengal, a reminder that infrastructure can carve empires as easily as swords.
